questions.prompt: The reaction time of 20 control-room operators is measured at the start and at the end of a 12-hour night shift. The 20 differences look roughly normal. Which test compares the mean reaction times?
options: Welch t-test on two samples of 20, with ν from its formula
Pooled t-test on two samples of 20, with 38 df
Paired t-test on the 20 differences, with 19 df
Two-sample z-test on two samples of 20, with no df
questions.explanation: Each operator is measured twice, so the data are paired: the start and end times of one operator share everything about that person. Test the 20 differences with the paired t-test, n − 1 = 19 df. The independent-sample tests would treat operator-to-operator variation as noise and lose the effect.

questions.prompt: Thirty bricks from kiln 1 and thirty different bricks from kiln 2 are tested for compressive strength. The sample standard deviations are 2.1 and 4.8 MPa; the population σ's are not known. Which test, with which degrees of freedom?
options: Pooled t-test, with n₁ + n₂ − 2 = 58 df
Welch t-test, with ν from the Welch–Satterthwaite formula
Paired t-test, with n − 1 = 29 df
Two-sample z-test, with no degrees of freedom
questions.explanation: Independent samples (different bricks), σ unknown, and a variance ratio of 4.8²/2.1² = 5.2, far above the course's 2 to 3, so equal variances cannot be assumed. Welch's t-test does not pool; its degrees of freedom come from ν = (a + b)²/[a²/(n₁ − 1) + b²/(n₂ − 1)] with a = s₁²/n₁ and b = s₂²/n₂.

questions.prompt: Two batches of epoxy are tested for peel strength (N/mm). Batch 1: n₁ = 10, x̄₁ = 52.3, s₁ = 4.1. Batch 2: n₂ = 9, x̄₂ = 48.9, s₂ = 2.6. Calculate Welch's t statistic for H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = 0. Give it to two decimals.

Sixteen strain gauges were read before and after a calibration change. The differences have mean d̄ = 1.8 µε and standard deviation s_d = 2.4 µε. Calculate the paired t statistic for H₀: μ_d = 0. Give it to two decimals.
questions.explanation: t = d̄/(s_d/√n) = 1.8/(2.4/√16) = 1.8/(2.4/4) = 1.8/0.6 = 3.00, with n − 1 = 15 degrees of freedom. The two-sided p-value is 2 × P(T > 3.00) with T on 15 df = 0.009.

questions.prompt: Before comparing the mean thickness of two independent samples of 15 films, an engineer gets: Shapiro–Wilk p = 0.41 and 0.63; Levene p = 0.003; s₁ = 1.2 µm and s₂ = 3.9 µm. What should she conclude about the assumptions?
options: Neither sample is normal: use the Mann–Whitney U test, not a t-test
Both samples look normal and the variances are equal: use the pooled t
Levene's p is small, so the means differ: no further test is needed
Both samples look normal, but the variances differ: use Welch, not the pooled t
questions.explanation: Shapiro–Wilk p-values of 0.41 and 0.63 give no evidence against normality. Levene's p = 0.003 is evidence that the variances differ (and s₂ is more than three times s₁). So a t-test is fine, but not the pooled one: use Welch. Levene tests the spreads, not the means.

questions.prompt: For a paired t-test on 12 pairs, which normality check is the right one?
options: Check that each of the two columns looks roughly normal
Check that the 12 differences look roughly normal
Check that the two columns have equal variances
No check: pairing removes the need for normality
questions.explanation: The paired t-test is a one-sample t-test on the differences, so it is the differences that must be roughly normal (box plot, Shapiro–Wilk). The columns themselves may be skewed or have different spreads; that does not matter to the paired test.

questions.prompt: A Welch test of two cooling-fan designs gives a 95 % confidence interval for μ₁ − μ₂ (airflow, m³/h) of −0.4 to 2.7. What is the decision of the two-sided test at α = 0.05, and why?
options: Reject H₀, because most of the interval is above 0
Reject H₀, because the interval is wider than 3
Do not reject H₀, because the interval contains 0
No decision is possible without the p-value
questions.explanation: A two-sided test at α rejects H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = 0 exactly when 0 is outside the (1 − α) confidence interval. Here 0 is inside, so p ≥ 0.05 and H₀ is not rejected. The interval also shows that differences up to 2.7 m³/h are still plausible: not rejecting is not the same as no difference.

questions.prompt: Two thousand pins from each of two machines are measured. The mean diameters differ by 0.02 mm, Welch's p = 0.001, and the specification is 10.00 ± 0.50 mm. Which statement is right?
options: The difference is large enough to matter for the specification, because p is very small
The difference is not real, because 0.02 mm is too small for any test to detect
p = 0.001 means there is a 0.1 % chance that the two machines are the same
The difference is real, but too small to matter for the specification
questions.explanation: With 2000 pins per machine, even a tiny difference is detected: p = 0.001 says it is probably real. But 0.02 mm is 4 % of the 0.50 mm tolerance; for the specification it hardly matters. A small p does not mean a large effect, and p is not the probability that H₀ is true.

questions.prompt: Nine welders each make one joint with rod A and one with rod B, and the joint strengths are compared. The nine differences include one far outlier, and Shapiro–Wilk on the differences gives p = 0.01. Which test should replace the paired t-test?
options: Mann–Whitney U test
Wilcoxon signed-rank test
Welch t-test
F-test for two variances
questions.explanation: The design is paired (each welder uses both rods) and the differences are not normal with a small n, so the paired t-test's assumption fails. The non-parametric test for paired data is the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, which ranks the sizes of the differences. Mann–Whitney is for independent samples.

questions.prompt: For a Mann–Whitney test, n₁ = 6 values from line 1 and n₂ = 7 from line 2 are ranked together. The ranks of line 1 add to R₁ = 30. What is U₁? It is a whole number.
questions.explanation: U₁ = R₁ − n₁(n₁ + 1)/2 = 30 − 6 × 7/2 = 30 − 21 = 9. Then U₂ = n₁n₂ − U₁ = 42 − 9 = 33. Under H₀ the mean of U is n₁n₂/2 = 21, so line 1 tends to have the smaller values.
